---
title: Additional Notes
---

## Sign-ins are not users

A sign-in count measures events. One person can sign in multiple times.

Use sign-ins when the question is about volume or system usage.

Use unique users when the question is about reach.

## Daily unique users are not the same as period unique users

Summing daily unique users gives a measure of user-days, not distinct people over the full period.

For distinct people over a longer period, use a cumulative unique user field such as `mtd_unique_users` or `ytd_unique_users`.

For a plain-language explanation of why the daily figures cannot be added, and why no unique-user count exists for an arbitrary window, see [Why Unique Users Cannot Be Added Up](unique-users.qmd).

## Metrics can be reported over different timespans

Most metrics are meaningful over more than one window. The three standard
reporting windows are month-to-date, year-to-date, and since the April 22, 2026
public launch. How you select a window depends on the kind of metric.

**Additive metrics** (sign-ins, MFA attempts, success rates, averages) are
computed by aggregating daily rows, so the window is just the date bounds in the
`WHERE CAST(from_date AS DATE) BETWEEN DATE '<start>' AND DATE '<end>'` clause. The same query
covers any window; only the start date changes:

- Month-to-date: first of the current month (for example, `2026-06-01`)
- Year-to-date: `2026-01-01`
- Since launch: `2026-04-22`

Set the end date to the reporting date.

**Cumulative unique-user metrics** cannot be derived by filtering a date range,
because summing daily `unique_users` counts user-days, not distinct people.
Instead, pick the pre-computed column that matches the window and take its
latest value:

- Month-to-date: `mtd_unique_users`
- Year-to-date: `ytd_unique_users`

Never sum these cumulative columns across rows.

There is no since-launch unique-user column. Additive metrics, such as
authentication events, SSO events, and MFA attempts, can be summed over any
window back to launch.

## Weighted averages should be used for call centre averages

When calculating average call length or average delay across multiple weeks, use a weighted average based on `calls_answered`.

A simple average of weekly averages may give too much influence to low-volume weeks.

## Internal applications should usually be excluded from external adoption reporting

Which applications count as internal is recorded in
[`rp.service.is_internal`](../catalog/rp/service.qmd), not in this document.
Resolve it through [`rp.alias`](../catalog/rp/alias.qmd), which maps the
application names IBM Verify and Google Analytics use back to a single service:

```sql
SELECT al.alias
FROM   rp.alias al
JOIN   rp.service s ON al.rp_id = s.rp_id
WHERE  s.is_internal
```

Query the list rather than pasting it into a filter. A service is reclassified
by editing the source spreadsheet, and a query holding its own copy of the list
will not notice. The same subquery works as a `NOT IN` in SQL and as an
`anti_join()` in dbplyr; both forms appear in
[SSO Events by Application](ibm_verify/sign-ins-by-application.qmd).

Whether to exclude internal applications at all depends on the reporting
question.

## External services with no recent traffic can be treated as inactive

An external service with no SSO events in the last three months can be treated
as inactive and left out of reporting, such as a count of integrated services or
a table with one row per service. It is still a relying party; it has nothing to
report. Say so wherever a count of services appears, because a reader cannot
tell a dropped service from one that never existed.

## The user ID "UNKNOWN" counts as one user

Some IBM Verify events carry the literal user ID `"UNKNOWN"` in place of a
pseudonymized one. The summary tables count it as one user in `unique_users`,
`mtd_unique_users`, and `ytd_unique_users`. Recipes that read the raw stream do
the same, so the two agree. It moves any count by at most one.
